summary:
TrueSouth is a web app that answers one question: where and when can a mission land on the Moon?

Near the lunar south pole the Sun stays within about two degrees of the horizon, Earth hangs low, and mountains block both. So whether a lander has power and a radio link depends on the exact site and date, and a launch slip changes the answer.

We built a pipeline that turns NASA's LOLA terrain and JPL Horizons positions into a skyline and an hourly record of the Sun and Earth over six years, for 25 sites and for any coordinates you type. Mission Control scores a landing date against a mission's rules and gives GO, CAUTION or NO-GO with the rule that decided it. Planners can slip the date, compare sites and explore 3D views. The Academy teaches the same physics in guided lessons.

Our Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons within 0.0061°.
details:
What it does and how it works TrueSouth tells a mission planner whether a lunar landing date works at a chosen site. A Python pipeline takes NASA's LOLA terrain and JPL Horizons positions and computes, for 25 sites, a skyline out to 300 km and an hourly record of the Sun and Earth for six years (2026 to 2031). The browser then scores any landing date against a mission's rules and gives GO, CAUTION or NO-GO, with the rule that decided it. Users can also type their own coordinates, which a server computes on demand.

It has two modes on the same data. Mission Control is for planners: a 3D view of the Moon, Earth and Sun, a polar map, a view from the lander's position, a timeline, a "Slip Planner" that shows every landing date for six years, and a Compare table. The Academy teaches the same physics in four guided lessons.

Benefits and intended impact Near the Moon's south pole the Sun stays within about two degrees of the horizon and mountains block it, so a short launch slip can turn a workable landing into a failed one. Existing tools show maps and positions; TrueSouth turns them into a decision in seconds, and shows why. We want planners to compare sites and dates quickly, and students and the public to understand why the south pole is hard.

Tools Python (NumPy, SciPy, pyproj, Pydantic, FastAPI) for the science and the server. TypeScript, React, Vite and three.js for the web app. pytest and vitest for tests, Docker for deployment. AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity) wrote and reviewed the code under the team's direction.

How it is creative It treats landing as a question of time, not only place. Slip the date and every site is re-scored at once; "Next GO" jumps to the next date that works; and the Slip Planner shows six years of landing dates for each site on one strip. The view from 2 m above the ground shows exactly which ridge hides the Sun, and Compare sets two sites at two dates side by side. Every mission number is marked as sourced or assumed, so a planner knows what to trust.

The same engine also teaches. In the Academy, a moon mascot called Luna guides learners through four short lessons to land a small lander: they drag the Sun through a month, sketch a skyline and see the real one laid over it, and find the bug in a calculation, all checked against the same real numbers a planner sees.

What we considered Honesty first. Every mission number is tagged as sourced or assumed. Our Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons within 0.0061°, and we publish the comparisons where we disagree with NASA's maps. Drawn shadows are decoration, never a result. We also considered speed on ordinary laptops and clear wording for non-specialists. TrueSouth is a planning aid, not flight certification.
